medium.titulo: Prompt caching is a prefix match. That explains almost everything.
medium.resumo: I started digging into how prompt caching works in Claude Code and realised I’d had the wrong picture all along.
medium.conteudo_html:
I started digging into how prompt caching works in Claude Code and realised I’d had the wrong picture all along.

I assumed my repo files were cached as separate pieces. Change a file, and that piece misses. Leave it alone, and it hits.

It turns out the API has no idea what a file is.

Everything Claude Code sends is one long sequence, and the cache matches it from the start. That one rule explains almost everything else. Why switching model is expensive and editing a file isn’t. Why Claude Code compacts instead of dropping old messages. And why a setting I had turned on was costing more than it needed to.

I run Claude Code against Claude on Bedrock, so I’ll point out where that differs. Numbers and limits are as of October 2026. They change, so check the docs before relying on them.

Every request resends everything

The Claude API is stateless. There’s no session on the server holding your conversation. Every request Claude Code sends contains the tool definitions, the system prompt, CLAUDE.md, the full message history and the new message. Turn 50 resends turns 1 to 49.

And a request isn’t one big string. It’s a list of content blocks:

{
  "tools":    [ {tool 1}, {tool 2}, ... ],
  "system":   [ {"type": "text", "text": "..."} ],
  "messages": [ {"role": "user", "content": [ ...blocks... ]}, ... ]
}

Each tool definition is a block. The system prompt is one or more text blocks. Each message is a container of blocks: text, images, a tool_use block when the model calls a tool, a tool_result block with what came back.

One question to Claude Code usually goes like this. Your message goes in. Claude replies with some thinking and a tool_use block, “read this file”. The result comes back as a tool_result. Repeat until Claude answers without calling a tool.

Your repo isn’t in the request

This was my misunderstanding. Claude Code doesn’t upload your repo, and it doesn’t send a set of “relevant files”. There’s no index.

A file only reaches the model when Claude reads it with a tool, or when you attach it with @. Either way, its contents land in a block in the message history, usually a tool_result. From then on it’s just part of the conversation, resent on every request.

So a file isn’t a cache entry. It’s text sitting somewhere in a long sequence.

In coding sessions, that reading is most of the context. I looked at my three largest Claude Code transcripts. Tool results (file contents, grep output, command output) made up roughly half of each one. Tool calls, including file contents Claude wrote, were another 20 to 30%. My own messages were a small share. These are character counts from the transcripts, so treat them as rough, but the pattern was the same in all three.

And changing a file doesn’t break anything. If Claude edits a file it read earlier, the old contents stay where they are in the history. Claude Code appends a note at the end saying the file changed, and Claude re-reads it if it needs to. Nothing earlier in the sequence moves, so the cache keeps hitting.

What gets cached

Claude Code assembles each request in a fixed order, with the things that rarely change first:

┌───────┬────────┬───────────┬──────────┬───────┬─────┬─────┐
│ tools │ system │ CLAUDE.md │ env info │ msg 1 │ ... │ new │
│       │ prompt │ / memory  │ + git    │       │     │ msg │
└───────┴────────┴───────────┴──────────┴───────┴─────┴─────┘
 position 0 ─────────────────────────────────────────────► end

The client marks some blocks with cache_control. These are breakpoints, and a request can currently have up to four.

A breakpoint doesn’t cache just the block it sits on. The cache entry is keyed on everything from position 0 up to and including that block.

tools ─ system ─[BP1]─ msg1 ─ msg2 ─[BP2]─ msg3 ─[BP3]
key(BP1) = hash(tools + system)
key(BP2) = hash(tools + system + msg1 + msg2)
key(BP3) = hash(tools + system + msg1 + msg2 + msg3)

So a breakpoint isn’t a separately cached chunk. It’s a checkpoint on one continuous sequence. Change one byte in the system prompt and all three miss, even though every message is identical. Change something in msg3 and only BP3 misses.

Multiple breakpoints are really a fallback. If the conversation part breaks, the tools and system prompt can still come from cache.

Why a prefix? Because of what’s being saved. It isn’t embeddings, which are a cheap table lookup. It’s the work the model did on the start of the prompt: the keys and values every layer computes for every token. Above the first layer, those depend on everything that came before. They also depend on the token’s position. So the same text after a different prefix, or in a different place, doesn’t produce the same state.

You can reuse a prefix. You can’t reuse a chunk from the middle.

Anthropic’s docs don’t say exactly what they store. OpenAI’s are more explicit: their prompt cache stores KV tensors.

Four breakpoints, 20 positions of lookback

If a request only has four breakpoints, how does a long conversation keep hitting the cache? I was confused by this at first.

They’re two different things:

  • Four breakpoints is how many markers one request can carry. “Cache up to here.”
  • 20 positions is how far back from each marker the server will look for an entry an earlier request already wrote.

The cache isn’t limited to four entries. Every previous request left one behind at its own marker. On the next request the marker has moved forward. The server finds nothing at the new marker, steps back position by position, and hits the previous request’s entry.

Request N:    tools ─ system ─ m1 ─ m2 ─ m3 ─[BP]
              writes an entry at m3
Request N+1:  tools ─ system ─ m1 ─ m2 ─ m3 ─ m4 ─ m5 ─[BP]
              nothing at m5, walk back ◄── found m3
              read up to m3, compute m4–m5, write at m5

In the usage numbers, a healthy request looks like this:

cache_read_input_tokens       97.3k
cache_creation_input_tokens    1.2k
input_tokens                   2

97.3k read from the previous entry, 1.2k of new content written, 2 tokens not cached at all.

On the Claude API, a run of consecutive tool_use blocks counts as one position, and so does a run of tool_result blocks, so a burst of parallel tool calls costs about two. Bedrock’s docs just say “approximately 20 content blocks”. Either way, if more than that gets added between two cache writes, you miss even though nothing changed. Claude Code moves its marker on every request, so this rarely bites. In your own agent loop it can. The API also has automatic caching, which places and moves the breakpoint for you.

Lifetime and cost

Cache entries expire. There are two lifetimes, 5 minutes and 1 hour. Every read resets the timer at no extra cost, so an active session keeps its cache warm. Step away for longer than the TTL and the next request rebuilds everything. The timer runs from the start of the request, not the end of the response, so a long generation uses up part of it.

Claude Code picks the TTL based on how you pay. On a subscription, within your plan’s included usage, the main conversation gets 1 hour. On usage credits, an API key or a cloud provider like Bedrock, it’s 5 minutes. On Bedrock, 1-hour availability also varies by model.

Each model has its own cache. On the Claude API caches are isolated per workspace. On Bedrock, per organisation.

Here are Opus 5.5 list prices on the Claude API, per million tokens. Bedrock’s pricing is set by AWS, so check yours, but the shape is what matters:

  • Fresh input: $4.00 (1×)
  • Cache write, 5-minute: $5.00 (1.25×)
  • Cache write, 1-hour: $8.00 (2×)
  • Cache read: $0.20 (0.05×)

The usual rule of thumb is that reads cost a tenth of input. That’s still true on Sonnet 5.5. Opus 5.5 is cheaper again, at a twentieth.

Writes cost more than normal input, so caching only pays off when content gets reused. With the 5-minute cache you’re ahead on the second use, with the 1-hour cache on the third. A Claude Code session clears that easily.

What really costs money is a miss. If 100k tokens miss and get written back to the 1-hour cache, that’s $0.80 instead of $0.02 for a read. Forty times more. With the 5-minute cache it’s 25 times.

On a subscription you don’t see these dollars, but the same tokens count against your plan usage.

What breaks it

Once you think of caching as a prefix match, you can predict what breaks it. Anything that changes content near the start invalidates everything after it.

In Claude Code, the main ones are:

  • Switching model. Different model, different cache. That includes opusplan, a model setting that uses Opus while you’re in plan mode and Sonnet when it’s executing. Every time you enter or leave plan mode, the cache starts cold.
  • Changing effort. On most setups this starts a fresh cache. Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Fable 5.1 keep it, but only with an API key or a subscription. Not on Bedrock, which means not for me. If you just want more thinking on one hard question, type ultrathink in your prompt instead. It adds an instruction to your message rather than changing the effort level, so the cache is untouched.
  • Turning on fast mode. It adds a header that’s part of the cache key. Once per conversation.
  • Upgrading Claude Code. A new version usually changes the system prompt or tools, so your first session after an upgrade starts cold.
  • Lots of images. When a request would pass the image limit, Claude Code drops a batch of the oldest ones, and everything from there on is reprocessed.
  • Going idle past the TTL. On a 5-minute TTL, a coffee break is enough.
  • Compaction. More on that below.

Just as useful is what doesn’t break it. Connecting an MCP server mid-session usually doesn’t, because tool search keeps the tool list fixed from the first request. Editing CLAUDE.md doesn’t either. It’s read once at session start, so your edit doesn’t invalidate the cache, but it also doesn’t apply until /clear, /compact or a restart.

And because the working directory and git status are near the start of every request, two sessions in different directories never share a cache. Two running in parallel in the same directory do.

If you’re building on the API yourself, the same rule tells you how to lay out a prompt. Stable content first, volatile content last. No timestamps or request IDs in the system prompt. One changing value near the top quietly turns every request into a miss.

Subagents

Each subagent is a separate conversation with the API, with its own context window, its own system prompt, and possibly a different model.

So a subagent doesn’t use the main conversation’s cache. It builds its own, and in Claude Code it gets the 5-minute TTL by default, even on a subscription. That default makes sense. Subagents work in quick bursts and then they’re done, so a 1-hour write would pay for time nobody uses. The main conversation is the opposite, because humans pause.

Forks are different. A fork is a subagent that starts with a copy of your whole conversation, so its request is your cached prefix plus a new task, and it reads the parent’s cache.

The main conversation isn’t disturbed by a subagent. Its result comes back as a new block at the end, so the main prefix stays intact. But while a long subagent runs, the main conversation sits idle. If it’s on a 5-minute TTL and the subagent takes longer than that, the main cache can expire before you get back to it.

This is where I found my own mistake. On Bedrock the main conversation defaults to 5 minutes, so I had set ENABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_1H=1. It looks like the obvious switch. But it applies to both the main conversation and everything outside it: subagents, compaction, workflows. So I was paying the 1-hour write price on requests that never needed it.

The setting I actually wanted was CLAUDE_CODE_PROMPT_CACHE_TTL=1h, or promptCacheTtl in settings, which only covers the main conversation. Everything outside it has its own control, subagentPromptCacheTtl. You can check which TTL your main conversation is actually using with claude -p "hello" --output-format json, which splits cache writes into 1-hour and 5-minute tokens.

Side requests: the fast model and prompt suggestions

Not every request Claude Code sends is part of your conversation.

Some are background work on a smaller, cheaper model. Claude Code calls it the background or “fast” model, and by default it’s Haiku. The ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL setting controls it, and the docs describe it as the model for “background functionality”. The examples given are summarising past conversations for claude --resume and status checks behind commands like /usage.

Beyond that, it isn’t really documented. I couldn’t find a full list of what runs on the fast model, or how much of your conversation those requests carry. What the prefix rule does tell you is that a different model means a different cache. Whatever these requests send, they can’t read your main conversation’s cache.

Prompt suggestions are the opposite case, and my favourite example of Claude Code designing around the cache. After each response, Claude Code sends a short request to suggest your next prompt. You’d expect that to go to the cheap model. It goes to your main model instead.

That looks backwards until you remember the prefix rule. The suggestion request is your conversation plus a small instruction at the end, so on the main model it’s almost entirely cache reads and a few output tokens. On Haiku, it would be the whole conversation processed from scratch. The expensive model is the cheap option here. (The docs confirm it reuses the cache. The reasoning is my read of why.)

Claude Code skips suggestions when you’re close to your usage limit, and you can turn them off.

Compaction, and why there’s no sliding window

With a 1M token window it’s tempting to never compact. But caching makes a big context cheap per token, not per request. At 800k tokens, every request still reads 800k tokens from cache. On Opus 5.5 that’s $0.16 per request before any new input or output, and a session can have hundreds of requests.

/compact replaces the history with a summary. If the cache is still warm, it’s cheaper than it sounds. The summary request reads the old history from cache, and the rebuild afterwards only covers the short summary. If the cache has already gone cold, the summary request reprocesses the full history at full price. So compact at a natural break while you’re still working, not when you come back the next morning.

If you just want to abandon a wrong turn, /rewind is cheaper still. It cuts the history back to a prefix that’s already cached.

You might wonder why Claude Code doesn’t just drop the oldest messages as the context fills up. A sliding window would change the start of the conversation on every request. With a prefix cache, every request would miss.

Compaction breaks the cache too, but once. Then the shorter history gets cached and keeps hitting. Clearing the contents of old tool results works the same way: one rebuild, not one per request.

Seeing it yourself

Claude Code’s status line runs a command of your choice and pipes session info to it as JSON. Since v2.1.251 that includes a prompt_cache object with the session’s cache stats, alongside the token counts from the last API call. Miss causes need v2.1.260 or later.

You don’t need to write the script by hand. I described what I wanted and let Claude Code build it with /statusline. Mine looks like this:

/ (master) [Opus 5.5] │ ctx 2% used │ $0.32 (turn $0.02)
cache │ hit ratio 87% │ last call: read 24.5k · write 237 · uncached 2 │ 1h ttl · warm until 14:32 │ misses 0

last call is the prefix rule in action: almost everything read, a little new content written. warm until moves out with every request.

The hit ratio is session-wide, which is why I care more about misses. An 87% ratio can hide one expensive miss. Claude Code counts a miss when a request re-processes a meaningful chunk of content the cache already held (more than 5% and at least 2,000 tokens), unless a compaction explains it. It also records a likely cause, like tools_changed or ttl_expired_5m. My line shows the cause next to the count.

The dollar figures are Claude Code’s own estimate at list price. On Bedrock, your actual bill can differ.

If you don’t want a custom status line, /usage shows the session’s hit ratio, miss count and whether the cache is warm. Either way, the stats only cover the main conversation, not subagents.

The part worth watching is what happens when a session sits idle past its TTL. Here’s an illustration: a session with about 100k tokens of context, on the default 5-minute TTL.

While you’re working, every request reads the previous one’s cache:

cache │ hit ratio 92% │ last call: read 98.1k · write 1.2k · uncached 3 │ 5m ttl · warm until 12:04 │ misses 0

Then you go to lunch. At 12:04 the cache expires, and Claude Code re-runs the status line on its own:

cache │ hit ratio 92% │ last call: read 98.1k · write 1.2k · uncached 3 │ 5m ttl · cold, next call re-caches 99.3k │ misses 0

next call re-caches 99.3k is Claude Code telling you how big the prefix is that it will have to rebuild. That’s roughly the 98.1k that was read plus the 1.2k that was written on the last call. Nothing has been charged yet.

You come back and send a message:

cache │ hit ratio 88% │ last call: read 0 · write 99.6k · uncached 3 │ 5m ttl · warm until 13:10 │ misses 1 (last: ttl_expired_5m)

Nothing was read. The whole conversation was written to the cache again, plus your new message. On Opus 5.5 at the 5-minute write price, that one request cost about $0.50 in input. Reading the same tokens would have cost about $0.02.

And look at the hit ratio. It only dropped from 92% to 88%, because it’s averaged over the whole session. The miss count is what tells you something expensive just happened, and the cause tells you why.

medium.titulo: Using Claude Code for SEO: From Existing Data to Work You Can Review
medium.resumo: SEO work often involves moving between reports, pages, and different kinds of decisions. A team compares search performance, investigates…
medium.conteudo_html:
SEO work often involves moving between reports, pages, and different kinds of decisions. A team compares search performance, investigates declining pages, prepares briefs, reviews internal links, and checks proposed technical changes. Much of the time is spent collecting and organizing the information before a decision can be made.

Claude Code can help with those activities when it has the relevant files or connected tools and a clearly defined assignment. Ahrefs’ guide presents 35 use cases across content, performance analysis, research, publishing checks, technical work, and monitoring.

The useful starting point is a task whose output can be inspected. Comparing two exports, identifying missing questions in an article, or proposing links with exact locations gives the reviewer something concrete to assess. The examples below adapt the supplied guide into a workflow-oriented explanation. Reported experiences belong to the people described in the source; they are not universal performance benchmarks.

Define the question and the deliverable

“Improve SEO” leaves the scope open. “Compare these two reports and show the five pages with the largest click losses” defines a result that can be checked. The assignment should identify the data, period, selection rule, and required columns.

The deliverable should also match its audience. A content team may need related queries and questions to investigate. A technical team may need the affected URL, current setting, and intended behavior.

Specify whether the work involves analysis, recommendations, or a proposed edit. These are different outputs. A comparison table can be produced without changing the website. A shared-template change needs code review and checks on the affected pages.

This definition makes later review more efficient. The team can evaluate whether the task was completed instead of interpreting an open-ended summary as evidence of improvement.

Start with files you already understand

Search Console exports, crawl data, page inventories, and article text can provide enough material for a first task. A small set of familiar files makes it easier to trace findings back to the inputs.

Claude Code is available through the Code section of the desktop application as well as other environments. The selected screenshot illustrates that workspace.

Direct connections can be added when they help a recurring workflow. APIs provide access to service data. MCP connects external tools and resources, while skills provide reusable instructions for an activity.

Those components serve different purposes. A well-written skill does not supply missing data, and a connected tool does not define the question. The assignment still needs a clear scope and a reviewable output.

Compare complete periods before investigating declines

Choose two complete periods of equal length and keep important filters comparable. Ask for prior clicks, current clicks, absolute change, and percentage change by page.

Absolute and percentage losses answer different questions. A low-volume page can have a large percentage decline while contributing little to the site’s total loss. The report should state which measure determines priority.

Check a sample of the calculations. Missing rows, changed URLs, and a zero baseline need explicit treatment. The output should not hide those cases inside a simple ranking.

Then add impressions, position, and relevant queries for the important pages. A decline is a reason to investigate. Changes in demand, results layout, page content, and reporting completeness can lead to different next steps.

Use titles and click data to form hypotheses

High-impression pages with low click-through rates can be shortlisted for review. The thresholds should reflect the project and available data rather than being treated as universal standards.

Read the query, title, page content, and visible results together. A title may fail to describe a relevant answer, or competing results may meet the searcher’s task more clearly. Other search features can also affect the visible layout.

Ask for alternatives alongside the current title, with a reason for each suggestion. The revised wording should describe what the page actually delivers. A promise about tested methods or a specific number of items needs support in the content.

Monitor the result after a change. A new title is a proposed improvement, not a guaranteed increase in clicks. A before-and-after observation also needs context before it is presented as causal evidence.

Read paid and organic search together

The guide describes three useful comparisons: paid terms with strong organic presence, paid terms with weak organic visibility, and organic terms absent from the campaign list.

The first group can support investigation of advertising’s additional effect. A good organic position does not establish that the ad is unnecessary. The second group may provide content-research candidates, while the third may offer ideas for paid tests.

Match terms using comparable periods and keep spending, organic presence, and recorded actions beside each entry. Note any differences between the reports.

The resulting table supports discussion between teams. It does not decide profitability or campaign settings automatically. The offer, destination page, conversion measurement, and test results still matter.

Connect search performance to page-level outcomes

Search reports describe visibility and clicks. Website analytics can describe recorded actions after arrival. Matching by page can help identify destinations associated with inquiries, purchases, or another defined outcome.

Check dates, URL formats, and event definitions before joining the reports. A measurement change can alter the apparent result. The analysis should make that change visible.

Keep the conclusion at the supported level. These reports do not identify the sale produced by every individual query. Search clicks and analytics visits also have different definitions and should not be treated as identical counts.

Engagement needs context as well. A short visit may complete a simple task. Review the purpose of the page and the platform’s measurement rules before interpreting an exit as a failure.

Decide whether the idea needs a new page

A new keyword can point to a need that an existing article already covers. Give Claude the page inventory, relevant content, and search data, then ask it to identify useful passages and candidate pages.

A reviewable output can recommend creating a page, improving an existing one, or rejecting the idea. Each recommendation needs a reason and the relevant URL.

The distinction depends on the reader’s task. Similar wording can represent different needs, and different wording can describe the same need. The proposed grouping should be reviewed against the actual pages.

This also applies to cannibalization. Two pages appearing for one query do not automatically justify deletion or merging. Examine their purpose, content, links, and performance before changing their roles.

Build content around evidence the team already has

Expert interviews, product demonstrations, and documented experience can provide material beyond the existing ranking pages. Claude can organize a transcript, suggest an outline, and prepare a draft.

Ask specific questions before recording the interview. Customer objections, common mistakes, limitations, and suitability can produce useful details. A vague conversation may lead to an equally vague article.

During editing, compare the draft with the transcript. Preserve the speaker’s actual view, and remove statements attributed to them that they did not make.

The same approach can help with an archive. Claude can identify related passages across old articles or a manuscript. Those passages still need review for accuracy, freshness, and relevance to the current assignment.

Make the editorial stages inspectable

The selected skills table separates research, outlining, drafting, claim verification, and publishing preparation. It also shows a distinct sequence for updating content.

For each stage, define the input, output, and acceptance criteria. Preserve intermediate results so the reviewer can inspect where a weak final draft began.

If the research lacks evidence, generating another draft may not resolve the problem. If the outline misses the main question, sentence-level editing will not repair the structure.

The guide reports a short draft-production time for one established pipeline. That is a specific workflow result. Other teams need to account for their own research, review, and publication requirements.

Consider a small tool when the task calls for calculation

Some searches are well served by a calculator, converter, or another interactive tool. Claude Code can help write the initial implementation when the inputs and logic are defined.

The second screenshot describes an open-source project introduced by a Reddit user. It combines keyword research, publishing, and interactive tools.

Treat that post as the user’s reported experience. For your own tool, define units, formulas, rounding, and invalid-input handling.

Test normal and edge cases using independent expected results. The surrounding page should explain the conditions of the calculation. A tool that looks polished but returns unreliable answers does not meet the reader’s task.

Adapt research to the format people will use

A tutorial video can become an article with written steps, headings, and screenshots. Provide the transcript, audience, and intended search questions. Then compare the draft with the recording.

An article can also support a video script. Spoken explanations need a suitable pace, examples, and visual cues. Reading every paragraph unchanged may produce an awkward recording.

The 78% figure in this screenshot concerns buying-related answers in that person’s limited review. It should not be described as the share of all Google AI answers.

Short posts and community answers need their own requirements too. Each version should answer the relevant question independently and preserve important conditions when the original research is shortened.

Research competitors without copying their publishing plan

Competitor pages can reveal questions your site has not covered. Ask for a topic list with evidence, the relevant source pages, and a reason the topic matters to your customers.

Search-result research can also support a brief. Record common questions, examples, and page formats. Then identify the original expertise or evidence your own article can contribute.

Local pages need genuine service availability and useful local information. A list of service-location combinations should be reviewed before it becomes a publishing queue.

Comparison pages require accurate information about both options. Features, pricing conditions, suitability, and switching considerations should be supported. The draft should expose gaps in the available information rather than fill them with invented claims.

Find outreach opportunities with a clear relevance test

The guide includes discovery work for comparison articles, journalist requests, and original research. Claude can organize opportunities and prepare material for review.

For each opportunity, record why the team is relevant. A competitor’s appearance in an article is not sufficient evidence that your product should be included.

For journalist requests, check the question, deadline, and the team member’s actual expertise. A proposed response should be reviewed by someone who can stand behind its facts and experience.

For research, preserve the data-collection method and calculations. Patterns can be useful findings, but they do not automatically demonstrate cause and effect. The published explanation should keep that distinction clear.

Check business facts, style, and evidence before publication

Use an up-to-date reference for approved names, features, prices, and conditions. Claude can compare the draft with that reference and flag inconsistencies.

Recurring editorial rules can become separate checks. Missing sections, prohibited wording, required formatting, and repeated closing phrases are examples of reviewable criteria.

Evidence checking should link factual claims to the material supporting them. Geographic scope, dates, audiences, and measurement definitions need attention.

Titles should also be compared with the content. The search title, main heading, and sharing title do not need identical wording, but their promises should be consistent with what the page provides.

Give internal-link recommendations exact locations

A useful recommendation identifies the source page, destination, passage, and proposed anchor. This is more actionable than a list of URL pairs.

Review whether the link helps the reader at that point. The next step may be a supporting guide, a product detail, or another practical explanation. It should follow the context.

Check crawl coverage before interpreting a page as orphaned. Missing data can make the link picture incomplete. Backlink information can provide additional context about common entry pages.

After implementation, inspect the live link and destination. The proposed wording should remain natural in the sentence, and the reader should reach a valid, useful page.

Use technical findings as an evidence-based review list

Provide crawl data, response headers, page code, canonical destinations, redirects, and sitemap entries where relevant. Ask for affected URLs and the specific conflict.

A noindex instruction can appear in page markup or a response header. Canonicals and redirects need valid destinations. Sitemap entries should be compared with the current site’s intended indexable pages.

Some exclusions and redirects are deliberate. Confirm the intended behavior before changing them.

For multilingual pages, review equivalent destinations and reciprocal references. Structured data needs both valid syntax and accurate information matching the page. A template-level change should be tested on several affected pages.

Performance work should connect a report finding to the relevant code. Review the proposed edit, confirm the page still works, and repeat the test under comparable conditions.

Keep changes and outcomes in the same operational history

Record what changed, when, why, and who was responsible. Titles, sections, links, and technical settings can all become useful context during a later performance review.

Claude can compare that history with search data and identify changes worth investigating. A change preceding a decline is a clue, rather than proof of causation.

A weekly report can summarize the affected page, supporting numbers, observed change, and next question. Add an owner and status for the actionable items.

Begin with one task and inspect several runs. Once the output is useful and consistent, turn the successful method into a reusable instruction. The record of each run then helps the team improve the process and understand the recommendations it receives.

Prepared by the specialized SEO team at EhsanKhosravi.com (SEO Manager, Specialist, and Strategic Consultant).

medium.titulo: 53 Seconds Down To 0.6: The One-Line Nuxt 4.6 Change Worth Testing This Week
medium.resumo: The gain shows up in Nuxt’s own benchmark on large route sets. Here is how to try it safely, plus the other 4.6 changes worth your time.
medium.conteudo_html:
The gain shows up in Nuxt’s own benchmark on large route sets. Here is how to try it safely, plus the other 4.6 changes worth your time.

In Nuxt’s own benchmark, a type check that took 53.63 seconds and then failed with a TS2589 error now finishes in 0.62 seconds. The change behind it is one config line, and it is part of Nuxt 4.6, a release with over 420 commits that its authors describe as one of their biggest minor releases. It also brings Vapor Mode support, portable server code, built-in sessions, and a faster dev server. That’s a lot of surface area, and almost none of it is mandatory, which is exactly why it’s easy to start in the wrong place.

Before the walkthrough, where this kind of work usually gets planned. Nuxt 3 has now reached end-of-life, and teams still on it often bring in Vue.js Migration Services to sequence the move to Nuxt 4. Products that also carry AI features in the interface tend to pair that with AI web application development and AI SaaS development. A recent read, Vue.js 2026: The New Standard for High-Performance Frontend Development, covers the wider Vue toolchain well.

The Headline Number, And The Honest Caveat

Typed $fetch and useFetch have long been typed from your server routes. Past a few hundred routes, though, TypeScript hit its instantiation limit and threw TS2589: Type instantiation is excessively deep. Nuxt 4.6 rebuilds this on a new foundation, so the cost now scales with how many call sites you have, not how many routes exist.

Peak memory for those same runs dropped from 946 MB to 140 MB.

The caveat: these are Nuxt’s own figures from generated route sets, and most apps have far fewer routes than the bottom rows. Notice the top row, though. Even at 100 routes the check got faster, and the larger gain is that the error disappears at scale.

Turn It On In Three Steps

Step one: upgrade, on a branch.

bash

npx nuxt upgrade --dedupe

This release requires Node.js ^22.22.3, ^24.15.0, or 26 and above, so check your runtime first.

Step two: opt in. On Nuxt 4 this is experimental and off by default, because it slightly changes type inference. It becomes the default in Nuxt 5.

ts

// nuxt.config.ts
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  experimental: {
    routeTypedFetch: true,
  },
})

Step three: see what it catches. The route set now carries the body, query, and headers each handler validates, so a wrong payload becomes a compile-time error instead of a runtime surprise:

ts

// server/api/users.post.ts validates { title: string, count: number }
await $fetch('/api/users', { method: 'post', body: { title: 'a', count: 'no' } })
//                                                              ^ not assignable to number

Expect two small changes when you switch it on. A Date returned by a handler is typed as a string at the call site, and any hand-written ServerRoutes augmentations need a small rewrite. There is also an optional experimental.strictRouteTypes setting that rejects calls to paths that don't exist.

The Other Changes Worth Your Time

One gotcha deserves its own warning. On Nuxt 4, the auto-imported defineEventHandler, getQuery, and readBody are still h3's own helpers, which take a different event shape. To use the new server runtime, import from nuxt/server explicitly, including defineEventHandler. Mix the two and you'll see a NUXT_E8012 error that tells you which import to change.

ts

// server/api/hello.ts
import { defineEventHandler, getQuery } from 'nuxt/server'
export default defineEventHandler((event) => {
  const { name } = getQuery<{ name?: string }>(event)
  return { message: `Hello, ${name ?? 'world'}!` }
})

Nothing in this release requires migrating server code. It’s an opt-in path for teams who want portability ahead of Nuxt 5.

Try Nuxt 5 Defaults Without Waiting

Most of what’s coming in Nuxt 5 is already in 4.6, either on or behind a flag. One setting turns the Nuxt 5 defaults on together, and you can still toggle each one individually:

ts

export default defineNuxtConfig({
  future: {
    compatibilityVersion: 5,
  },
})

Where Each Change Pays Off

  • SaaS dashboards and back offices, where hundreds of API routes make typed $fetch the biggest single win
  • Fintech and banking portals, where catching a wrong payload shape at compile time is cheaper than catching it in production
  • E-commerce storefronts, where link-heavy pages benefit most from the SSR throughput gains
  • Media and publishing sites, where pages carry many internal links and server rendering cost adds up
  • Any team still on Nuxt 3, where the end-of-life notice turns a “someday” migration into a planned one

What I’d Do This Week

  1. Upgrade on a branch and run your type check before and after, so you have your own numbers
  2. Turn on routeTypedFetch and fix whatever the new strictness surfaces
  3. Leave Vapor for a fresh project until the Vue 3.6 stable release lands
  4. If you’re on Nuxt 3, put the migration on the calendar instead of the someday list
  5. Leave nuxt/server for when you next touch server code, since it's optional

Roughly how many API routes does your Nuxt app have, and has TS2589 ever shown up in your editor? Tell me in the comments, I'm curious where people actually sit on that table.

medium.titulo: How to Add Multiple Languages to Laravel + Inertia.js Without Managing Translations Twice
medium.resumo: Build multilingual applications with Laravel, Vue 3, React, or Svelte using one set of translation files.
medium.conteudo_html:
Build multilingual applications with Laravel, Vue 3, React, or Svelte using one set of translation files.

Laravel has always made localization fairly straightforward. You create your language files, define translation keys, and use Laravel’s __() helper wherever you need translated text.

But things become a little different when your frontend uses Inertia.js with Vue, React, or Svelte.

Laravel understands your PHP translation files. Your frontend components don’t automatically have access to them.

And that’s where a simple multilingual feature can start requiring more work than expected.

In this article, I’ll show you how to use your existing Laravel language files directly in Inertia.js components, without maintaining separate translation files for your frontend.

The Problem with Localization in Laravel + Inertia.js

Imagine you’re building a dashboard using Laravel and Vue 3.

In your Laravel application, you have a translation file:

lang/en/messages.php

<?php
return [
    'welcome' => 'Welcome back!',
    'dashboard' => 'Dashboard',
    'settings' => 'Settings',
];

In Laravel, using those translations is easy:

__('messages.welcome');

But what happens when you want the same translation in a Vue component?

<template>
    <h1>{{ __('messages.welcome') }}</h1>
</template>

That won’t work automatically. Vue doesn’t know anything about Laravel’s translation files.

You could install a separate internationalization library, maintain JavaScript translation objects, or manually share translations through Inertia middleware.

All these approaches can work.

The problem is that you may end up managing the same text in two different places.

When you add another language or update a translation, you have more files to maintain.

For applications with dozens of pages and hundreds of translation keys, that becomes difficult to manage.

A Simpler Approach: Laravel Lang Sync Inertia

To make this easier, I built an open-source package called Laravel Lang Sync Inertia.

The idea is simple: Laravel already knows which language your application is using, and it already has your translation files.

Why not reuse those translations in your frontend?

With this package, you can select your Laravel translation files and share them with Inertia.js using a single helper:

syncLangFiles('messages');

Your frontend can then access those translations using familiar helpers:

__('messages.welcome')

The package currently supports:

  • Laravel translation files shared through Inertia.js.
  • Vue 3, React, and Svelte frontend components.
  • Dynamic placeholders such as :name.
  • Pluralization using transChoice().
  • Nested translation files and dot-notation keys.
  • Automatic loading based on Laravel’s active locale.
  • TypeScript-compatible frontend helpers.
  • Optional PHP-to-JSON translation export.

Let’s build a working example.

Step 1: Install the Package

First, install the Laravel package using Composer.

composer require erag/laravel-lang-sync-inertia

Next, install its frontend companion package:

npm install @erag/lang-sync-inertia

If your Laravel application doesn’t already have published language files, run:

php artisan lang:publish

Then run the package installation command:

php artisan erag:install-lang

This publishes the package configuration and required assets.

You now have what you need to start sharing Laravel translations with your Inertia frontend.

Step 2: Create Your Language Files

Let’s support English and Hindi in our application.

Inside Laravel’s lang directory, create the following files:

lang/
├── en/
│   └── messages.php
└── hi/
    └── messages.php

English: lang/en/messages.php

<?php
return [
    'dashboard' => 'Dashboard',
    'welcome' => 'Welcome back, :name!',
    'settings' => 'Settings',
    'notifications' => '{0} No notifications|{1} One notification|[2,*] :count notifications',
];

Hindi: lang/hi/messages.php

<?php
return [
    'dashboard' => 'डैशबोर्ड',
    'welcome' => 'वापस आने पर स्वागत है, :name!',
    'settings' => 'सेटिंग्स',
    'notifications' => '{0} कोई सूचना नहीं|{1} एक सूचना|[2,*] :count सूचनाएं',
];

We’re using Laravel’s normal PHP translation structure.

There are no separate JavaScript translation files to maintain.

And if you already have Laravel translations in your project, you can reuse them.

Step 3: Share Translations from Your Laravel Controller

Now open the controller that renders your Inertia page.

For example, DashboardController.php:

<?php
namespace App\Http\Controllers;
use Inertia\Inertia;
use Inertia\Response;
class DashboardController extends Controller
{
    public function index(): Response
    {
        syncLangFiles('messages');
        return Inertia::render('Dashboard');
    }
}

That’s the important part:

syncLangFiles('messages');

The helper loads the selected language file based on Laravel’s active locale and shares its translations through Inertia.

You don’t need to create a separate API endpoint or manually pass every translation through your controller response.

You can also share multiple language files when needed:

syncLangFiles([
    'messages',
    'auth',
    'validation',
]);

This is useful for larger applications, where you might have different translation files for authentication, dashboards, settings, and other modules.

Instead of loading everything everywhere, you can choose the files required by each page.

Step 4: Use Laravel Translations in Vue 3

Now let’s display those translations in our Vue dashboard.

Open resources/js/Pages/Dashboard.vue.

<script setup lang="ts">
import { vueLang } from '@erag/lang-sync-inertia';
const { __, trans, transChoice } = vueLang();
</script>
<template>
    <main>
        <h1>{{ __('messages.dashboard') }}</h1>
        <p>
            {{ trans('messages.welcome', {
                name: 'Amit'
            }) }}
        </p>
        <p>{{ __('messages.settings') }}</p>
        <p>
            {{ transChoice('messages.notifications', 3) }}
        </p>
    </main>
</template>

When Laravel’s active locale is English, the page displays:

Dashboard
Welcome back, Amit!
Settings
3 notifications

When the active locale is Hindi, the same component displays:

डैशबोर्ड
वापस आने पर स्वागत है, Amit!
सेटिंग्स
3 सूचनाएं

Notice something important.

We didn’t change the Vue component to support Hindi.

The translation keys remain exactly the same.

Laravel determines the active language, and the package makes the matching translations available to Vue.

That’s the behavior I wanted when building this package.

Step 5: How Language Switching Works

One important thing to understand is that Laravel Lang Sync Inertia uses Laravel’s current locale.

For example:

use Illuminate\Support\Facades\App;
App::setLocale('hi');
syncLangFiles('messages');

This loads the Hindi translations for that request.

For a real application, you would normally store the user’s selected language in a session, user preference, or similar location.

Then, your Laravel middleware can set the locale on each request before the controller loads translations.

The package handles sharing the appropriate translations. Your application remains responsible for deciding which language the user wants.

When Inertia receives updated page props for the new locale, the frontend helpers can use the new translation values.

That keeps language selection separate from translation delivery.

Step 6: What About React and Svelte?

Although we’ve used Vue 3 in this example, the package isn’t limited to Vue.

The Laravel implementation stays the same.

You only need the frontend helper for your chosen framework.

React example

import { reactLang } from '@erag/lang-sync-inertia';
export default function Dashboard() {
    const { __, trans } = reactLang();
    return (
        <main>
            <h1>{__('messages.dashboard')}</h1>
            <p>
                {trans('messages.welcome', {
                    name: 'Amit'
                })}
            </p>
        </main>
    );
}

Svelte 5 example

For Svelte, use @inertiajs/svelte v3.

<script module lang="ts">
    import { svelteLang } from '@erag/lang-sync-inertia';
    const { __, trans } = svelteLang();
</script>
<main>
    <h1>{__('messages.dashboard')}</h1>
    <p>
        {trans('messages.welcome', {
            name: 'Amit'
        })}
    </p>
</main>

The translation keys, language files, and Laravel controller remain unchanged.

So whether you build your frontend with Vue, React, or Svelte, you can continue using the same Laravel localization structure.

Step 7: Organizing Translations in Larger Applications

As your application grows, keeping every translation in one file becomes difficult.

You might want a structure like this:

lang/
└── en/
    ├── auth.php
    ├── messages.php
    └── admin/
        ├── users.php
        └── settings.php

Laravel Lang Sync Inertia supports nested language directories.

For example:

syncLangFiles('admin.users');

Then in Vue:

__('admin.users.title')

This lets you organize translations by feature or module rather than putting everything in a single massive file.

For applications with multiple dashboards, administrative panels, or complex workflows, that organization makes a difference.

Bonus: Export Laravel PHP Translations to JSON

Sometimes you may want actual JSON translation files for a separate frontend workflow or build process.

The package includes an Artisan command for that too:

php artisan erag:generate-lang

By default, it generates frontend-ready JSON files under:

resources/js/lang/

The source and output paths can be customized in config/inertia-lang.php.

This feature is optional. You don’t need to generate JSON files to use the normal Inertia translation-sharing workflow.

Why Not Just Use Vue I18n?

That’s a fair question.

Vue I18n is a mature solution with capabilities that extend beyond simply sharing Laravel translations. If your application already has a frontend-specific internationalization architecture, it might be exactly what you need.

Laravel Lang Sync Inertia solves a more focused problem.

If Laravel is already your source of truth for translations, you may not want to maintain another set of language files just for Vue.

With this package, Laravel continues managing translation data, while Inertia makes selected translations available to the frontend.

It isn’t about replacing every internationalization library.

It’s about removing duplicated work for developers using Laravel and Inertia together.

A Few Things Worth Remembering

Before using localization in a production application, keep a few practical details in mind:

  • Make sure the requested locale is supported by your application.
  • Use a middleware or another per-request mechanism to restore the user’s selected locale.
  • Share only the translation groups needed by your page.
  • Prefer Laravel’s :name placeholder syntax for new translations.
  • When changing languages, ensure Inertia receives fresh page props for the selected locale.

These small decisions make multilingual applications easier to maintain as they grow.

Final Thoughts

Adding another language to an application shouldn’t mean rewriting the same translations in multiple places.

If you’re already using Laravel with Inertia.js, you have most of the localization infrastructure you need.

The missing piece is making those translations available to your frontend components in a clean, consistent way.

That’s why I created Laravel Lang Sync Inertia.

It’s open source, and I hope it saves other Laravel developers some of the repetitive setup involved in building multilingual applications.

If you’re working with Laravel, Vue 3, React, or Svelte, give it a try.

Resources

  • GitHub: https://github.com/eramitgupta/laravel-lang-sync-inertia
  • Documentation: https://erag.in/laravel-lang-sync-inertia/
  • Composer package: https://packagist.org/packages/erag/laravel-lang-sync-inertia
  • Frontend package: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@erag/lang-sync-inertia

If you find it useful, consider starring the GitHub repository. And if you run into an issue or have an idea for improvement, feel free to open an issue.

Thanks for reading!

— Amit Gupta

corrida_no_ar.resumo: Analisamos os números da Maratona de Chicago, com participação feminina recorde. Abordamos a polêmica do tempo do Strava versus o oficial, além da revolta por falta de água na Maratona de Melbourne e na Meia Maratona Lopes Guarulhos.
corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Terça-feira | 13 de outubro de 2026

A Maratona de Chicago de 2026 trouxe alguns números impressionantes. O mais surpreendente foi a participação feminina: 45,8% dos concluintes foram mulheres, contra 53.8% de homens. Esse é um dado que mostra uma aproximação cada vez maior das mulheres na distância da maratona, que historicamente tinha uma participação masculina muito maior, ao contrário das meias maratonas. A faixa etária com mais mulheres na prova foi a de 25 a 29 anos, com 5.608 concluintes, indicando que a Geração Z está chegando com força total às maratonas e começando mais cedo na distância. Entre os homens, a faixa mais representativa foi a de 30 a 34 anos.

Outro dado interessante é a presença internacional. O Brasil se consolidou como o quarto país com mais corredores na prova, somando 1.491 concluintes, ficando atrás apenas dos Estados Unidos, México, Grã-Bretanha e Canadá.

Polêmica do Strava: parem de postar tempo errado!

É preciso falar sobre uma prática que precisa acabar: postar nas redes sociais o tempo que o Strava marca para os 42,195 km em vez do tempo oficial da prova. A Maratona de Chicago é um exemplo clássico disso, pois é famosa por ter um sinal de GPS muito instável nos primeiros 8 km devido aos prédios altos, o que faz com que o relógio marque uma distância maior que a real.

O tempo que vale é o oficial, aquele cronometrado do pórtico de largada ao de chegada. É assim para a elite e é assim para todos. Divulgar o tempo do Strava, que quase sempre é menor por causa da marcação de distância imprecisa, acaba gerando desinformação. Em um exemplo recente, uma corredora postou o tempo de 3:08:55, mas seu tempo oficial foi de 3:11:05 — um tempo excelente, por sinal. O próprio Strava, no campo “tempo decorrido”, registrou 3:11:08, confirmando o resultado oficial. O tempo oficial é o que conta e é o que deve ser celebrado.

Revolta na Maratona de Melbourne

A Maratona de Melbourne, que teve a presença ilustre e a vitória de Eliud Kipchoge, foi alvo de duras críticas dos “Melbournenses”. A organização deixou muito a desejar em pontos básicos. Corredores relataram falta de água tanto nos postos de hidratação ao longo do percurso quanto na dispersão, após a linha de chegada. Além disso, houve queixas sobre a pouca quantidade de banheiros químicos, espaçamento inadequado dos postos de hidratação (que não estavam a cada 2,5 km como prometido) e ausência de placas de sinalização de quilometragem nos últimos 10 km. Para completar, formou-se um grande gargalo na chegada, com atletas esperando até 10 minutos para sair da área de dispersão.

Faltou água também em Guarulhos

O mesmo problema de falta d’água visto em Melbourne se repetiu na Meia Maratona Lopes Guarulhos. Corredores que participaram da prova de 21 km relataram que, a partir do km 14, já não havia mais água, obrigando-os a correr os quilômetros finais sem hidratação. Alguns chegaram a correr mais de 6 km sem água, e houve relatos até de quem desistiu da prova por conta disso. Em um vídeo, o organizador da prova afirmava que a estrutura só seria desmontada após a chegada do último corredor, mas os participantes criticaram duramente a falha na hidratação, que é um item essencial, especialmente em provas longas e com o calor que tem feito.
